metadata.title: American Mfrs. Mut. Ins. Co. v. Sullivan, 526 U.S. 40 (1999) (No. 97-2000)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: American Mfrs. Mut. Ins. Co. v. Sullivan

Opinion filed: 1999-05-24

Docket No.: 97-2000

Citations:
• 143 L. Ed. 2d 130
• 119 S. Ct. 977
• 526 U.S. 40
• 1999 U.S. LEXIS 1711

Case holding summaries:
• suspension of employee medical benefits
• explaining that extensive regulation does not convert a private company into a state actor liable under section 1983
• explaining that § 1983 actions do not reach purely private conduct
• explaining that such an allegation is the “first inquiry in every [procedural] due process challenge”
• "mere fact that a business is subject to state regulation does not by itself convert its action into that of the State"
• an employee must establish entitlement to payments under the relevant statute before litigating their withholding on constitutional grounds
• “The first inquiry in every due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in ‘liberty’ or ‘property.’”
• holding that ' 1983 liability requires state action
• explaining that the first inquiry is whether there has been a deprivation of property
• "Action taken by private entities with the mere approval or acquiescence of the State is not state action." (emphasis added)
• “The first inquiry in every due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in ‘property’ or ‘liberty.’” (quoting U.S. CONST . amend. XIV)
• liability under § 1983 requires showing that deprivation of federal right was committed under color of state law
• holding no state action and therefore no due process right to notice and opportunity to be heard before a private workers compensation insurer suspends payment of disputed medical bills pending a review of the reasonableness and necessity of injured employee’s medical treatment
• “Action taken by private entities with the mere approval or acquiescence of the State is not state action.” (emphasis added)
• “To state a claim for relief in an action brought under § 1983, respondents must establish that they were deprived of a right secured by the Constitution or laws of the United States, and that the alleged deprivation was committed under color of state law.”
• “To state a claim for relief in an action brought under § 1983, [plaintiffs] must establish that they were deprived of a right secured by the Constitution or laws of the United States, and that the alleged deprivation was committed under color of state law.”
• “The first inquiry in every [procedural] due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in ‘liberty’ or ‘property.’”
• finding state action when a defendant exercises a “right or privilege created by the State” (citation omitted)
• “[P]ermission of a private choice cannot support a finding of state action.”
• § 1983 22 actions do not reach purely private conduct
• “The first inquiry in every due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in property or liberty.”
• holding that “[a]ction taken by private entities with the mere approval or acquiescence of the State is not state action”
• describing function considered in West as “provid[ing] medical treatment to injured inmates”
• "The first inquiry in every due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in 'property' or 'liberty.'"
• “[T]he under-color-of-state-law element of § 1983 excludes from 10 its reach merely private conduct, no matter how discriminatory or wrongful.” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• “Action taken by private entities with the mere approval or acquiescence of the State is not state action.”
• "The first inquiry in every due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in `property' or `liberty.'"
• acknowledging that Lugar made clear that “its language must not be torn from the context out of which it arose” and therefore declining to extend Lugar where defendants made “no effort” to seize the plaintiffs’ property “by an ex parte application to a state official”
• plaintiff bringing action under § 1983 must show that he was “deprived of a right secured by the Constitution or laws of the United States”
• discussing the adoption of utilization review by Pennsylvania in 1993
• “To state a claim for relief in an action brought under § 1983, [plaintiffs] must establish that they were deprived of a right secured by the Constitution or laws of the United States, and that the alleged deprivation was committed under color of state law.”
• rejecting argument that state had delegated to insurers a “traditionally exclusive public function” to determine whether payment for disputed medical treatment should be suspended
• “[W]orkers’ compensation insurers are at least as extensively regulated as the private nursing facilities in Blum . . . . Like th[at] case[ ], though, the state statutory and regulatory scheme leaves the challenged decisions to the judgment of insurers.”
• “The first inquiry in every due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in ‘property’ or ‘liberty.’ ”
• “Action taken by private entities with the mere approval or acquiescence of the State is not state action.”
• linking the color-of-law element of 42 U.S.C. § 1983 to the underlying state-action requirement of the Fourteenth Amendment, and holding that both exclude from their reach "merely private conduct, no matter how discriminatory or wrongful"
• recognizing the property interests in Goldberg and Mathews
• holding that "[a]ction taken by private entities with the mere approval or acquiescence of the State is not state action"
• "To state a claim for relief in an action brought under § 1983, respondents must establish that they were deprived of a right secured by the Constitution or laws of the United States, and that the alleged deprivation was committed under color of state law. " (emphasis added)
• "‘[T]he party charged with the deprivation [of federally secured rights] must be a person who may fairly be said to be a state actor.’"
• “To state a claim for relief in an action brought under § 1983, [plaintiffs] must establish that they were deprived of a right secured by the Constitution or laws of the United States, and that the alleged deprivation was committed under color of state law.”
• liability under § 1983 requires showing that deprivation of federal right was committed under color of state law
• "`[T]he party charged with the deprivation [of federally secured rights] must be a person who may fairly be said to be a state actor.'"
• "The first inquiry in every due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in `property' or `liberty.'" (quoting U.S. CONST. amend. XIV)
• “Only after finding the deprivation of a protected interest do we look to see if the State’s procedures comport with due process.”
• "The first inquiry in every due process challenge is whether the plaintiff has been deprived of a protected interest in `property' or `liberty.'"
• “To state a claim for relief in an action brought under § 1983, respondents must establish that they were deprived of a right secured by the Constitution or laws of the United States, and that the alleged deprivation was committed under color of state law.”
• private insurer vested with the ability to "decid[e] whether to suspend payment for disputed medical treatment" not a state actor because such decisions not traditionally an exclusive governmental function
